Principles


The eight main points outlined in the Atlantic Charter


These foundational principles were established in 1941, during a time of great uncertainty and upheaval, by the leaders of the United States and the United Kingdom. The Atlantic Charter, as it came to be known, was a joint statement of the Allied powers' vision for a post-war world, one that would be guided by a set of core values and principles.


These principles were not simply a list of demands or a set of rules to be followed, but rather a comprehensive framework for understanding the nature of the world and our place within it. They were a call to action, a reminder that the decisions we make today will shape the course of history for generations to come.


The right of self-determination for all people


This principle is perhaps the most fundamental of all, for it recognizes that every individual and every nation has the inherent right to determine their own destiny. It is a recognition that we are all equal, that we all deserve to be treated with dignity and respect, and that we all have the right to shape our own futures.


In a world where the forces of oppression and tyranny have often sought to impose their will on others, this principle is a powerful reminder that we must always stand up for what is right, even in the face of overwhelming odds. It is a call to action, a reminder that we must always strive to create a world where every individual can live freely and pursue their dreams without fear of persecution or oppression.


The commitment to disarmament and collective security


In the aftermath of the devastating wars of the 20th century, it was clear that the world needed a new approach to security. The old model of nation-states competing for power and resources had led to catastrophic consequences, and it was time to think differently.


The commitment to disarmament and collective security represents a fundamental shift in our approach to the world. It recognizes that the pursuit of power and security is not a zero-sum game, where one nation's gain must come at the expense of another. Instead, it recognizes that true security can only be achieved through cooperation and mutual understanding.


This principle is not just a call to reduce our military spending or to eliminate certain types of weapons. It is a call to fundamentally rethink our approach to security, to recognize that our individual and collective security is inextricably linked to the security of others.


The promotion of economic cooperation and trade


In the aftermath of the Great Depression, the world was still reeling from the devastating effects of economic instability. The global economy was in shambles, and it seemed as though the very foundations of our societies were at risk.


The promotion of economic cooperation and trade represents a fundamental shift in our approach to the economy. It recognizes that our individual and collective prosperity is inextricably linked to the prosperity of others. It recognizes that the pursuit of economic growth and development is not a zero-sum game, where one nation's gain must come at the expense of another.


This principle is not just a call to reduce tariffs or to increase trade. It is a call to fundamentally rethink our approach to the economy, to recognize that our individual and collective prosperity is inextricably linked to the prosperity of others. It is a call to create a world where every individual can access the resources and opportunities they need to thrive, regardless of their nationality or background.
